1.10 Workflow: a photo library served from its previews

The previews plugin builds a browsable library out of files that already exist. Its guide is the complete reference; this section walks through a whole setup.

1.10.1 The idea

Suppose your originals are offline, but you have two smaller things for every photo:

  • a stand-in: a small DNG such as a Lightroom Smart Preview, which holds the photo’s metadata and a reduced raw image, but embeds only a tiny thumbnail;
  • a preview JPEG at a useful size, for example from an image browser’s preview cache, under a different name in a different folder.

An application that shows embedded previews, such as Photo Mechanic or Quick Look, shows only the thumbnail in the stand-in. The previews plugin serves each stand-in with its preview JPEG embedded, without writing or copying either file.

1.10.2 Building the stand-in tree

Arrange the stand-ins under the folder layout you want to browse, usually the originals’ layout. On APFS, use clones (cp -c) rather than copies: a clone shares its blocks with the original, so even a million stand-ins cost almost no disk space, and writing to a clone never changes the file it came from.

Then write a map file, one line per file to change, as a path relative to the tree followed by tab-separated fields:

2024/trip/IMG_0001.DNG  preview=a1/IMG_0001.jpg
2024/trip/IMG_0002.JPG  orientation=6   datetime=2024:10:02 04:45:42
2024/trip/IMG_0003.JPG  metadata=0/0A1B/0A1B2C3D.dng
Key For Value
preview DNG, TIFF The preview JPEG, relative to preview_root
preview_size DNG, TIFF Optional: the JPEG’s size in bytes
preview_mtime DNG, TIFF Optional: its modification time, SECONDS.NANOSECONDS
preview_dims DNG, TIFF Optional: its pixel size, WIDTHxHEIGHT
metadata JPEG A DNG whose EXIF and XMP the JPEG is served with, relative to metadata_root
orientation JPEG EXIF orientation, 1 to 8
datetime JPEG Capture time, YYYY:MM:DD HH:MM:SS

With all three optional preview fields, the server builds the disk without opening a million preview JPEGs, which makes startup much faster. They are still checked against the real file on every read.

1.10.3 What gets served

For a DNG or TIFF with preview=, every original byte stays at its original offset. The plugin appends a copy of the first image directory (IFD0) after the original data, adds one entry pointing at a new reduced-resolution image (a SubIFD), and appends the JPEG. Only the 8-byte TIFF header is changed, to point at the copied directory. Applications that show embedded previews then find the large JPEG; raw-capable applications still read the original image data. An existing large preview is kept and stays first.

For a JPEG, metadata= adds the EXIF and XMP of a DNG or TIFF, typically the photo’s Lightroom Smart Preview or an EXIF-only TIFF extracted with ExifTool, so the JPEG shows its camera, lens, exposure, serial number and GPS position. The plugin rebuilds the EXIF in a new segment, leaving out the DNG’s image-structure tags and maker note and adding the JPEG’s own pixel size. It reads the XMP segment’s contents from the DNG in place on every read, so they take no memory. The rebuilt EXIF, about 1.3 KB per JPEG, is kept in memory with the rest of the layout. orientation= and datetime= set Orientation and DateTimeOriginal in that segment, overriding the DNG, so portraits display upright and photos sort by capture time; they also work on their own.

A JPEG that already has EXIF, such as a Lightroom preview with Orientation and color space, has that segment replaced by the rebuilt one. The JPEG’s own tags win over the DNG’s, since they describe the preview’s pixels, and the map’s values win over both. Tags that describe pixels (color space, components, compression, pixel size, gamma) are never taken from the metadata file, even when the JPEG lacks them: a camera original’s sRGB says nothing about a preview rendered in Adobe RGB. Its own XMP is kept unless the DNG has XMP, which then replaces it.

Files not in the map are served unchanged. A mapped file that cannot be composed, because its JPEG is missing or the DNG has an unexpected structure, is served unchanged with a warning in the server log, rather than failing the disk.

1.10.4 The config

{
  "source": "/absolute/path/to/stand-in-tree",
  "plugin": "previews",
  "label": "Library",
  "writable": true,
  "plugins": {
    "previews": {
      "map": "/absolute/path/to/previews.tsv",
      "preview_root": "/absolute/path/to/preview-jpegs",
      "metadata_root": "/absolute/path/to/Catalog Smart Previews.lrdata",
      "ratings": "/absolute/path/to/ratings"
    }
  }
}

metadata_root is needed only when the map has metadata= fields. For a very large library, metadata_store can name one SQLite file holding all the metadata files as blobs in a table stubs(key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, exif BLOB), with metadata= giving the key; see the previews plugin guide. diskproxy reads the store itself, through SQLite bundled into the server, opened read-only and immutable, and refuses a store whose -wal file is not empty. Any SQLite writer can produce it. Tursolite, for example, can write it, optionally under Turso’s concurrent (MVCC) mode, and then seal it to an ordinary rollback-journal file that diskproxy can open. Leave out writable and ratings for a purely read-only library. Start it with diskproxy --config library.json start. Check one file through the mounted volume:

exiftool -b -PreviewImage /Volumes/Library/2024/trip/IMG_0001.DNG | wc -c

The result should be the size of its preview JPEG.

1.10.5 Capturing ratings

With ratings set and a writable view, the plugin reads each written file’s XMP metadata and keeps exactly four properties:

Property Meaning
xmp:Rating Star rating
xmp:Label Color label name
photomechanic:ColorClass Photo Mechanic’s color class
photomechanic:Tagged Photo Mechanic’s tag (flag)

Everything else an application writes is ignored. That is deliberate. Photo Mechanic, for example, sets creation dates from a file’s modification time when a JPEG has none, and copies the stand-in’s metadata into its XMP. Keeping its whole XMP block would carry those invented values back towards your originals.

The metadata is found in a JPEG’s XMP segment, a TIFF or DNG’s XMP tag, or an .xmp/.XMP sidecar. Each photo gets a minimal sidecar in the ratings folder, mirroring the tree:

Written file Sidecar
X.DNG, or its sidecar X.XMP X.xmp
X.JPG X.JPG.xmp, so a JPEG never collides with a DNG of the same name
A stand-in served as X.JPG.dng or X.RW2.dng Under the original’s name: X.JPG.xmp, X.xmp

A sidecar is rewritten only when a value changed. Every change is appended to JOURNAL.jsonl in the ratings folder, one JSON object per line:

{"time_unix":1793718040.97,"written":"2015/February/IMG_4193.dng",
 "sidecar":"2015/February/IMG_4193.xmp",
 "fields":{"xmp:Rating":"2","xmp:Label":"Red","photomechanic:ColorClass":"1","photomechanic:Tagged":"False"},
 "previous":{}}

written is the file the application wrote, sidecar the file updated in the ratings folder, and previous the values before this change. The ratings folder must be outside the served tree; the plugin refuses to start otherwise.

Clearing is captured too. When a file captured before is written without one of these properties, because the application removed it or its whole XMP block, the property is recorded as cleared (Rating 0, an empty Label, ColorClass 0, Tagged False), with the old value as previous.

Captured ratings outlive the session. The next time the disk is built, every served JPEG, DNG or TIFF with a sidecar is served with the sidecar’s values merged into its XMP packet. A DNG gets the merged packet appended after its data, through the same copied IFD0 that adds a preview. Only those four properties are replaced; the rest of the JPEG’s own or its metadata file’s XMP is kept, in one packet. An application that re-reads the file after a restart finds the ratings it wrote rather than losing them. The served modification time stays the source file’s.

These sidecars use the Adobe naming convention, so a DNG’s sidecar can later sit beside its original, where Lightroom or another application can read it. To bring the captured ratings into a Lightroom Classic catalog, follow the recipe in Lightroom Repair.

1.10.6 Two libraries served from previews

Two libraries have been built this way. The numbers are observations of each, not limits.

Smart Previews as stand-ins. On a laptop, a Lightroom Classic library’s Smart Previews were cloned into the originals’ folder layout as DNG stand-ins, and paired with Photo Mechanic’s 1600-pixel preview JPEGs: 671,335 DNGs gained the large preview, and 566,365 of 566,556 JPEGs gained the camera metadata of their Smart Preview, as metadata= files. The 1,256,465-file tree scanned in 110 seconds, about 50 seconds more than without metadata, and the server used 1.9 GB, about 1.3 KB more per mapped JPEG. The view is writable, with ratings captured as sidecars.

Regular previews with a metadata store. On a desktop, a Photo Mechanic catalog was built from APFS clones of Lightroom Classic’s ordinary preview levels, needing only the one drive that holds them. Camera metadata was extracted once, from an existing index of the originals’ metadata, as EXIF-only TIFFs written by ExifTool, and stored in one 3.8 GB metadata store of 834,891 entries. Half of these previews already carried a small Lightroom EXIF segment, merged as described above; most are Adobe RGB without an ICC profile, which is why pixel tags never come from the metadata. The 835,383 files in 6,521 folders scanned in 111 seconds on a busy machine (load average 11 to 15), and the server then used 1.64 GB.
